strengths: The proposed Diag-CFM modification is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained; the zero-anchoring idea directly addresses a real pathology (sensitivity of the bidirectional CFM formulation to coordinate ordering/scaling) in amortized inverse design.

The empirical evaluation is thorough: three datasets of increasing dimension (P=6 to P=100), 5 seeds per configuration, parameter-count-matched baselines (INN, standard CFM), an ordering ablation (Table 4) that directly validates the invariance claim, and an accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis (Figures 3, 5, 6) that anticipates and defuses the 'low diversity' objection rather than hiding behind raw diversity numbers.

The two UQ metrics are practical and well-differentiated from baselines: Zero-Deviation is free as a byproduct of generation, and the paper honestly reports the gap to oracle performance (34-57% for error-rejection) rather than overselling. The OOD detection setup (OOD points 2-8% of range from the training boundary) is a genuinely challenging and carefully constructed task.
Reproducibility is good: full architecture, optimizer, and dataset details are given in Appendices C-D, including INN baseline hyperparameters and the DTLZ stratified sampling scheme.
The limitations section is honest and specific (oracle gap, INN remaining competitive for forward prediction at P>=50), which increases trust in the reported results.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin. Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 are essentially one-line observations that follow immediately from the i.i.d. noise entries; calling the learning problem 'provably' invariant overstates the depth of the result, and the paper provides no theoretical link from permutation invariance of the target velocity to the observed order-of-magnitude accuracy gains - that connection is purely empirical.

The 'standard CFM' baseline is a somewhat non-standard formulation (flowing from [z;y] to x). While the bidirectional use case motivates it, the paper would benefit from a more careful discussion of why alternative conditional FM constructions (e.g., conditioning the vector field on y while flowing noise to x) are not applicable or fair, since the headline 'order-of-magnitude improvement over CFM' depends on this baseline choice. The INN baseline comparison is more convincing.

The UQ metrics are heuristic. Zero-Deviation and Self-Consistency are not validated as estimates of epistemic uncertainty per se (the aleatoric/epistemic framing in Section 3 is loose), no calibration analysis is provided, and several reported results are moderate rather than strong (OOD AUCs of 0.73-0.75 on Gas Turbine and DTLZ). No comparison to other general-purpose UQ baselines (MC dropout, conformal methods, density-based OOD scores) beyond ensembles and the FM loss.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed implementation appendix.

Originality is modest: zero-anchoring is a natural design fix rather than a new methodological framework, and the overall contribution is closest to an application/engineering paper (following Ardizzone et al. and Krueger et al.). This is acceptable but bounds the significance for the main track.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (reliable generative inverse design with abstention) and the proposed zero-anchoring modification to conditional flow matching is simple, clearly described, and easy to implement.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough: three datasets of increasing dimensionality (P=6, 14, up to 100), 5-seed repetitions, an ordering ablation (Figure 2, Table 4) directly supporting the stability claim, and accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis that preempts a natural criticism of raw diversity metrics.

The two architecture-intrinsic uncertainty metrics (Zero-Deviation as a free byproduct of generation, Self-Consistency) are practical and well-motivated by the bidirectional structure of the flow, and the UQ evaluation covers three distinct tasks (select-best, error-rejection, OOD detection) with honest oracle-gap reporting.
The limitations section is candid: the gap to oracle performance (34-57%) and the competitiveness of INN baselines for forward prediction at high dimension are acknowledged rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The central premise is questionable. The claimed 'instability' of standard CFM for inverse problems arises from the authors' own construction, which regresses design coordinates directly against label coordinates (Eq. 1). Standard conditional flow matching conditions on y rather than pairing x-coordinates with y-coordinates in this way, so the baseline appears to be a partially self-inflicted strawman. The paper does not establish that practitioners commonly use this formulation, which weakens the headline 'order-of-magnitude improvement over CFM' claim.

Limited technical novelty. Diag-CFM amounts to conditioning the flow on y and flowing noise to x with an extra zero-target output channel, and both Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 are near-trivial (invariance follows immediately from i.i.d. noise entries; Prop 4.2 from a degenerate coordinate alignment). The 'provably invariant' claim concerns only the target-velocity distribution, not the learned model, and the paper concedes this - so the theoretical contribution is thin relative to the framing.

The UQ contribution lacks theoretical grounding. Zero-Deviation and Self-Consistency are heuristics; no analysis connects them to epistemic uncertainty (e.g., why the zero-output channel should be a calibrated OOD signal). The baseline set for UQ is narrow (ensemble variance and FM loss only); obvious alternatives such as MC-dropout, likelihood/density-based scores, or kNN distance in label space are absent.

Round-trip error, the primary inverse-design metric, is evaluated against pre-trained neural surrogates for the two real datasets, introducing surrogate error into the ground truth; the sensitivity of conclusions to surrogate quality is not analyzed.

Results contain unexplained anomalies that reduce confidence: standard CFM is worst on forward MSE across nearly all settings (e.g., 10-25x worse than Diag-CFM), which is atypical and suggests possible baseline under-tuning; on DTLZ at P>=50, INN beats Diag-CFM on forward MSE, partially undercutting the generality claim. Table 4 numbers (CFM ranging 4.66e-3 to 3.02e-2 across orderings) are described inconsistently with the text ('nearly an order of magnitude').

Reproducibility is uncertain: implementation details are provided, but no code or data-release statement appears, and the augmented gas turbine dataset (200,000 samples) may not be publicly available.

Writing has rough edges: duplicated Rp references (e.g., Sec 3 defines latent z in R^{P-L} then notes 'suffice in principle' ambiguously), notation typos (s^{diag}_g), and repeated boilerplate passages between Sections 5.1 and Appendix E.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and previously under-appreciated failure mode of standard CFM when adapted to bidirectional inverse design: sensitivity to the arbitrary ordering and pairing of design and label coordinates. The proposed zero-anchoring fix (Diag-CFM) is simple, elegant, and well-motivated, and the accompanying Propositions 4.1/4.2 formally characterize the permutation equivariance of the target velocity distribution.

The empirical evidence is unusually thorough for this kind of method paper: three datasets of increasing dimensionality (P=6, 14, up to 100), an explicit ablation over four coordinate orderings (Table 4 / Figure 2) that directly validates the central claim, 5 seeds per configuration, parameter-matched baselines (~2.1M), and an analytical benchmark (DTLZ2) that allows exact round-trip evaluation without surrogate confounds. Reported gains are large (order-of-magnitude in round-trip error) and statistically supported.

The two architecture-intrinsic UQ metrics (Zero-Deviation, Self-Consistency) are novel, cheap (Zero-Deviation is a free byproduct of generation), and evaluated on three distinct, practically relevant tasks (select-best, error-rejection, OOD detection) with oracle upper bounds and correlation statistics reported honestly. The paper does not overstate: it reports where baselines win (e.g., FM Loss on Unifoil OOD), where correlations are modest, and where Ensemble Variance beats the proposed metrics.

The accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis (Section 5.1, Appendix E) is a thoughtful methodological contribution in itself, exposing why raw diversity metrics can be misleading when comparing generative models of differing accuracy.
The limitations section is candid and specific (gap to oracle 34-57% for error-rejection, INN competitiveness for forward prediction at P>=50), which builds trust in the reported results.
weaknesses: The OOD detection evaluation is missing its most obvious baseline. OOD targets are constructed by label-space distance to the nearest training point (normalized distance 2-8%); a simple kNN-distance or KDE score in label space would presumably achieve near-oracle AUC by construction, yet is not compared. Without it, the claim that Zero-Deviation 'consistently outperforms general-purpose alternatives' for OOD detection is not fully established.

Round-trip error on two of three datasets (gas turbine, Unifoil) is measured against pre-trained surrogate models rather than the underlying physics. All methods are trained on labels generated by these surrogates, so the evaluation is internally consistent, but the surrogate-based ground truth introduces a possible circularity (e.g., surrogate bias regions could differentially favor methods whose generated designs cluster in particular ways). The DTLZ2 results mitigate but do not fully remove this concern.

The theoretical contribution is modest. Propositions 4.1/4.2 only establish (non-)equivariance of the target velocity distribution; they do not directly explain the observed training stability and accuracy gains, and the paper is appropriately careful to say so, but this leaves the gap between theory and the empirical claims bridged only by the single-dataset ordering ablation (gas turbine only).

The magnitude of the CFM baseline's failure deserves closer scrutiny: CFM's round-trip error being 10-30x worse than a coupling-based INN on some configurations suggests the baseline may be under-tuned (e.g., conditioning architecture, normalization choices), so some of the reported advantage could reflect baseline weaknesses rather than the zero-anchoring fix itself.

The UQ gains, while consistent, are moderate in absolute terms: Pearson correlations of 0.2 (Unifoil, DTLZ P=100) and error reductions of 8-14% on several datasets, versus oracle improvements of 34-94%. Self-Consistency is near-random on DTLZ P=100 OOD (AUC 0.51), which somewhat undercuts the 'consistently outperforming' framing for that metric.

No code release is mentioned, and despite detailed hyperparameters, reproducibility of the dataset augmentation pipelines (200,000-sample gas turbine set, stratified DTLZ sampling) is uncertain without released artifacts.

Overall, the core methodological idea (anchor labels to zero, pair designs with noise) is simple. The value lies in the identification of the problem and the breadth of validation rather than in a deep new technique, which limits the conceptual significance for a main-track venue.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: zero-anchoring (pairing design coordinates with noise and labels with zero) removes the spurious dependence of CFM's regression target on the arbitrary ordering of design and label coordinates, with short proofs (Props. 4.1/4.2) establishing that the Diag-CFM target velocity is permutation-equivariant while standard CFM's is not.

Unusually thorough empirical validation: five datasets spanning P=6 to P=784, an ordering ablation (Appendix B) directly supporting the invariance claim, surrogate-robustness checks with noise injection and nine independent surrogates (Appendix D), ODE solver sensitivity sweeps (Appendix E), accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis that guards against a misleading diversity metric, and physical OOD tests (negative drag, extreme L/D, below drag-polar) in Appendix H.3.

The UQ contribution is practical and well-argued: Zero-Deviation is free at generation time, and the paper honestly reports oracle gaps (34–57%) and cases where baselines (Ensemble Variance) fail or where INN beats Diag-CFM on DTLZ forward prediction at P≥50.

Reproducibility is strong: a reference implementation with runnable examples is promised, implementation details are extensive, and evaluation protocols (5 runs, held-out test sets, fixed seeds) are stated. Limitations are discussed candidly.
weaknesses: The key baseline may be a strawman. The paper's 'standard CFM' formulation transports labels as flow coordinates ([z; y] → x), but the far more common conditional FM formulation conditions the velocity field on y* (vθ(t, x; y*)) and never subtracts labels from design coordinates in the loss. This trivially avoids the permutation/scale-mismatch pathology the paper attacks, yet no such conditioning baseline (nor SBI-style conditional flows, nor DFlow-SUR) is compared. The headline 'order-of-magnitude gains over CFM' therefore do not establish gains over the most natural competing approach.

Novelty is modest: the method is essentially a reparameterization/anchoring trick, and Proposition 4.1 only shows the target velocity distribution is permutation-equivariant — it neither implies the learned model is invariant nor explains why zero-anchoring improves absolute accuracy. The accuracy gains are purely empirical and the causal mechanism is asserted from observation ('we observed a strong dependence on ordering') on a single dataset.

The permutation-sensitivity phenomenon is demonstrated only on the gas turbine dataset; claims that heterogeneous-scale datasets 'would likely be more pronounced' are speculative and unverified. Gains elsewhere are much smaller (thin film: 1.3–1.7×; FashionMNIST round-trip: 1.5×), so the generality of the central claim is unevenly supported.

Round-trip error for two of the five datasets (gas turbine, Unifoil) is measured against learned surrogates rather than the true simulator, so the headline inverse-design accuracy metric is partly circular. The robustness checks in Appendix D mitigate but do not eliminate this concern.

UQ results are mixed in absolute terms: Zero-Deviation AUC is 0.75 on gas turbine and 0.73–0.82 on DTLZ in the hard setting, and select-best correlations are sometimes weak (ρ=0.20–0.21); practical value at these levels is arguable.

Presentation defects: the sentence 'unlike the flow matching loss zero-deviation requires no extra model evaluations' is garbled, Figure 2's axis labels are unreadable, the Unifoil surrogate input dimension (16 vs P=14) is inconsistent with the stated basis dimension, and the code URL is missing from the availability statement.

strengths: The core idea (zero-anchoring: pairing design coordinates with noise and labels with zero in the flow-matching loss) is simple, clearly motivated, and addresses a genuine practical problem: the CFM loss couples coordinates of heterogeneous meaning and scale, and the paper demonstrates empirically that performance depends on arbitrary ordering decisions (Figure 2, Table 6).

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: five tasks spanning P=6 to P=784, an ordering ablation with 5 seeds per ordering, accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis (a thoughtful correction to naive diversity metrics), ODE solver sensitivity sweeps (Appendix E), surrogate-output noise and cross-surrogate robustness checks (Appendix D), and physically grounded OOD tests for Unifoil (negative drag, extreme L/D, below-drag-polar, conditioning shift).

The two UQ metrics (Zero-Deviation, Self-Consistency) are cheap, architecture-intrinsic, and Zero-Deviation in particular comes free with generation; the experiments honestly report the gap to oracle performance (34-57% for error-rejection) rather than overselling.
Limitations are discussed candidly (INN competitive on DTLZ forward prediction at high P, distance-to-oracle gap), and a reference implementation is provided.
weaknesses: The baseline definition is questionable and central to the claims. The paper's 'standard CFM' transports the joint state [z; y] -> x, which is one particular (and arguably non-standard) way to adapt CFM to inverse problems. The more conventional formulation treats y as a conditioning variable of the vector field (as in SBI-style flow matching, which the authors themselves cite), which would not exhibit the ordering/scale sensitivity between x and y that motivates Diag-CFM. Without a conditioned-flow baseline, it is unclear whether the large gains over 'CFM' reflect the zero-anchoring fix or the weakness of a specific, somewhat strawman formulation.

Novelty is thin. The theoretical contribution (Propositions 4.1 and 4.2) is trivial - equivariance of a target velocity distribution under permutations where Z has i.i.d. entries is nearly immediate, and the proof of the negative result is a one-line counterexample. Presenting these as headline contributions overstates the work. The practical modification amounts to a re-pairing of the coupling, and no comparison is made against more recent generative inverse-design methods (e.g., DFlow-SUR is cited but not compared).

The claimed 'provably invariant learning problem' is weaker than the language suggests: the paper itself concedes this only establishes that the class of required functions is the same across orderings, not that training dynamics, initialization sensitivity, or convergence are invariant. The abstract and contribution list could mislead readers.

The UQ results are modest in the most challenging settings: Zero-Deviation AUC is 0.73-0.77 on the hard near-boundary OOD tasks for gas turbine and DTLZ, and select-best improvements over random selection (5-31%) capture only a fraction of the 81-94% oracle potential. The paper acknowledges this, but the practical significance of 'abstention' at these performance levels is limited.

Presentation issues: the Code Availability statement appears truncated (no visible URL), Figure 2's axis labeling is hard to parse, and the primary narrative leans on relative speedup factors ('6.5x', 'order of magnitude') where absolute error levels and their engineering relevance for the heterogeneous label sets (e.g., thermoacoustic growth rate G) are not discussed.

Some benchmarks feel artificial relative to the engineering motivation: the FashionMNIST image-statistics task (P=784) tests scalability but has little connection to design problems, and the DTLZ2 experiments use a non-standard stratified sampling scheme whose effect on comparisons is not ablated.

strengths: The core idea — zero-anchoring labels and pairing all design coordinates with noise — is simple, well-motivated, and the permutation-equivariance argument (Propositions 4.1/4.2 with proofs in Appendix A) cleanly formalizes why the standard CFM augmented-space formulation is ordering-sensitive.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: five datasets spanning P=6 to P=784, including one with an exact analytical forward map (TMM thin film) and one beyond MLP design spaces (CNN on FashionMNIST statistics), with 5-seed averaging throughout.

The paper anticipates and addresses many reviewer concerns via appendix experiments: an ordering ablation (Figure 2/Table 6), ODE solver sensitivity sweep (Appendix E), surrogate-output noise injection and 9-surrogate cross-validation for round-trip robustness (Appendix D), and accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis that avoids the misleading 'higher diversity is better' trap.

The two architecture-intrinsic UQ metrics (Zero-Deviation, Self-Consistency) are practically attractive — Zero-Deviation is free as a byproduct of generation — and the OOD experiments include physically grounded infeasibility tests (negative drag, below drag-polar), not just synthetic label-space perturbations.
Honest limitations section (gap to oracle of 34-57%, DTLZ forward-prediction losses to INN at P>=50) and a stated reference implementation support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest. The 'instability' of standard CFM is largely an artifact of the authors' own augmented-space construction ([z; y] -> x), and the fix (flowing [z; y] -> [x; 0]) essentially recovers the structure already used by coupling-based INNs, which are included as a baseline. A skeptical reader may see Diag-CFM as a sensible engineering choice rather than a fundamentally new method; Propositions 4.1/4.2 are elementary.

Missing comparison to the most closely related flow-matching approach: Wildberger et al. (2023) apply flow matching to simulation-based inference with the target as a conditioning variable — arguably the natural CFM-based alternative formulation — yet it is discussed in Related Work but not benchmarked. The 'standard CFM' baseline may be a weak strawman relative to what an expert would actually deploy.

The UQ metric comparisons are limited to four metrics and one ensemble size (M=5); no comparison against other single-model UQ baselines (e.g., MC dropout, likelihood/density-based scores), so the claim that the proposed metrics 'consistently outperform' general-purpose alternatives rests on a narrow baseline set. Ensemble Variance in particular may be handicapped by construction (it measures dispersion of forward predictions of the same candidate, not generation quality).

Two of five datasets (gas turbine, Unifoil) evaluate round-trip error via learned surrogates; while Appendix D checks robustness, some reported gaps (e.g., Unifoil round-trip 1.68e-3 vs 3.82e-3 for INN) are within ranges that surrogate error could plausibly affect, and the gas turbine 'ground truth' is itself surrogate-generated data (200k augmented samples), raising questions about what is actually being learned.

Some presentation and reporting issues: Table 2 INN diversity standard deviation (+-2.19e-2) exceeds its mean (1.44e-2), which is unexplained; abstract claims 'order-of-magnitude gains on several benchmarks' while thin film gains are only 1.3-1.4x; the code availability URL is missing/empty in the manuscript.

The DTLZ forward-prediction regression to INN at P>=50 (up to ~8x worse MSE) is explained only speculatively ('may be a product of the nature of this dataset'), leaving an uncharacterized boundary condition on when the method helps.
